h: Bonnie Dundee, a railway viaduct and Queen Victoria's view
p: The battle in 1689 was a short and bloody affair. Jacobite forces led by John Graham of Claverhouse, Viscount Dundee, better known as 'Bonnie Dundee', charged down on government troops under General Hugh Mackay and routed them. It should have been a famous triumph, but Dundee was mortally wounded in the fighting, and without him the rising soon ran out of steam. Knowing that twist makes a walk through the pass feel all the more poignant.

The gorge has drawn visitors for a long time. Queen Victoria passed through in the 1840s and was taken with the scenery, and a little further west the famous Queen's View looks out along Loch Tummel, a lovely stop if you're driving. Keep an eye out too for the railway viaduct that carries the Highland main line across the gorge, a proper bit of Victorian engineering that looks wonderful framed by the trees.

Allow at least a couple of hours if you'd like to walk down to the river and see the Soldier's Leap, longer if you fancy following the paths further along the Garry towards the Linn of Tummel. Bring a flask and something to sit on, because there are some cracking spots to pause and listen to the water.

Blair Castle, the white-walled seat of the Dukes of Atholl, is just a few miles north at Blair Atholl and makes a natural partner on the same day. Heading the other way, Pitlochry has its dam and fish ladder, where salmon make their way upstream in season, plus plenty of cafés and shops along the main street.
